title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
text:
Today

The problem — data in the wrong zones
Support — what does a value attached to a polygon mean?
Extensive vs. intensive — what happens when you split a geometry?
Areal interpolation in R — st_interpolate_aw() and st_agr()
Limitations — when the uniform assumption fails; dasymetric mapping

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
text:
Data in the wrong zones
You have data — but the zones don’t match what you need:

Population by canton, but you need it by biogeographical region
Income by census tract, but you need it by school district

The source zones and target zones overlap in arbitrary ways. You cannot simply reassign values — you have to redistribute them.

Areal interpolation is the second largest source of error in spatial data science.

Edzer Pebesma - Areal interpolation methods - useR! 2026

Students often assume this is a rare edge case. It is not. Any time you combine data from different administrative sources — census, tax, health, transport — you face this problem. The error compounds silently: results look reasonable but are systematically wrong.

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
text:
The core challenge


Walk through the problem: target zone X overlaps with all of A and half of B. You cannot just assign A’s population to X — X also covers part of B. You need to split B’s population between X and Y based on how much of B falls in each target zone.

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
section: Q1: What does the value refer to?
text:
Q1: What does the value refer to?
Before you can redistribute a variable, you need to know what it represents.

Point support — the value refers to each individual location: E.g. Land cover, soil type
Block support — the value refers to the whole geometry as a unit: E.g. Population count, average income


Point-support variables can be sampled and re-aggregated without conceptual difficulty. Block-support variables cannot — they are aggregates, and their spatial distribution within the polygon is unknown. Areal interpolation only applies to block-support variables.

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
text:
Why support matters

For point-support variables: you can query any sub-region directly. A raster crop, a spatial filter, a point-in-polygon lookup — all valid.
For block-support variables: the value only makes sense for the whole geometry. Splitting it requires an assumption about how the variable is distributed within the polygon.

The simplest assumption: uniform distribution — the variable is spread evenly across the area.
This assumption is almost never true

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
section: Q2: What happens when you cut a polygon in half?
text:
Q2: What happens when you cut a polygon in half?
Question: does the value sum across sub-regions, or does it stay constant?



Variable
Cut in half →
Type




Population count (1 000)
~500 each
Extensive


Population density (50/km²)
still 50/km² each
Intensive


Total household income (€200M)
~€100M each
Extensive


Average household income (€60k)
still €60k each
Intensive


Number of schools (12)
~6 each
Extensive


School density (2/km²)
still 2/km²
Intensive




Extensive = summable = total. Intensive = per-unit = rate or density or average. The confusion between the two is a classic error in spatial analysis — e.g. summing population densities instead of averaging them, or averaging population counts instead of summing them.

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
text:
Redistribution formulas


Extensive (counts, totals — the sum must be preserved):
\[v_j = \sum_i v_i \cdot \frac{\text{area}(A_i \cap B_j)}{\text{area}(A_i)}\]
Each source value is split proportionally to the area of intersection.

Intensive (rates, densities, averages — no sum to preserve):
\[v_j = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_i v_i \cdot \text{area}(A_i \cap B_j)}{\displaystyle\sum_i \text{area}(A_i \cap B_j)}\]
Each source value is weighted by the intersection area, then averaged.


How to read the formulas — use the toy example (A/B/C → X/Y):

\(i\) indexes source zones (A, B, C); \(j\) indexes target zones (X, Y)
\(v_i\) is the value in source zone \(i\) (e.g. 900 people in B)
\(A_i \cap B_j\) is the intersection of source zone \(i\) with target zone \(j\) (e.g. the left half of B that falls in X)
\(\text{area}(A_i \cap B_j) / \text{area}(A_i)\) is the area fraction — what share of source zone \(i\) overlaps target zone \(j\). B∩X = 50%, so 0.5 × 900 = 450.

Extensive: sum contributions from all source zones touching \(j\), each scaled by area fraction. For X: 100%×600 + 50%×900 = 1 050.
Intensive: area-weighted average — weight each source value by how much of the target it covers. For Y: B covers 1 unit, C covers 2 units → (60×1 + 70×2)/3 = 66.7 k.
Key contrast: extensive preserves the total (1 800 in, 1 800 out). Intensive preserves the scale of the variable (still CHF/year, not CHF·km²/year).

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
text:
st_interpolate_aw()

# extensive = TRUE  →  sum-preserving (counts, totals)
pop_by_target <- st_interpolate_aw(src["population"], tgt, extensive = TRUE)

Warning in st_interpolate_aw.sf(src["population"], tgt, extensive = TRUE):
st_interpolate_aw assumes attributes are constant or uniform over areas of x





Notice the warning: assumes attributes are constant or uniform over areas of x
This is the uniform distribution assumption — built into the method.

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
text:
When the uniform assumption fails
The uniform distribution assumption is wrong whenever the variable is spatially heterogeneous within the source zone.
Examples:

Population in a municipality that is 80% forest → people cluster in villages, not forest
Income data for a large canton → urban and rural areas have very different incomes
Large source zones intersecting many small target zones → fine-grained heterogeneity is lost

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
text:
Dasymetric mapping

Improve accuracy by using ancillary data that captures spatial heterogeneity within the source zone.
Classic example — population redistribution:

Overlay source zones with land use / building footprint data
Assign population only to residential areas
Intersect with target zones and sum

The more precise the ancillary layer, the more accurate the result.
In R: pass the ancillary layer as weights = to st_interpolate_aw().
Example from r-spatial.github.io/sf


Dasymetric mapping is the standard improvement over naive areal weighting. It’s especially important when source zones are large relative to the variation in the variable. The key limitation: you need a good ancillary layer, which itself may be outdated or imprecise.

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
section: Intensive vs extensive — side by side
text:
Intensive vs extensive — side by side

nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
g  <- st_make_grid(nc, n = c(10, 5))

a1 <- st_interpolate_aw(nc["BIR74"], to = g, extensive = FALSE)
a2 <- st_interpolate_aw(nc["BIR74"], to = g, extensive = TRUE)
sum(a2$BIR74) / sum(nc$BIR74)   # mass preserved → 1

[1] 0.9999998




Intensive and extensive give visually different results even on the same data. The extensive result preserves the total count (ratio → 1). The intensive result does not — it spreads values as if they were uniform rates, so the sum drifts. This is the core reason the distinction matters.

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
text:
Dasymetric mapping in R

grd.addr <- read_sf(system.file("gpkg/grd_addr.gpkg", package = "sf"))
nc2 <- st_transform(nc, st_crs(grd.addr))
st_agr(grd.addr) <- c(ones = "constant")
st_agr(nc2)      <- c(BIR74 = "constant")

bir0 <- st_interpolate_aw(nc2["BIR74"], to = grd.addr, extensive = TRUE)
bir1 <- st_interpolate_aw(nc2["BIR74"], to = grd.addr, extensive = TRUE,
                           weights = "ones")
sum(bir1$BIR74) / sum(nc2$BIR74)   # mass preserved → 1

[1] 1

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Today

Centroids — center of mass, and when it lies outside the polygon
Affine transformations — shift, scale, rotate with sf arithmetic
Simplification — Douglas-Peucker, topology problems, ms_simplify()
Challenge — design a line simplification algorithm

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Center of mass

st_centroid() returns the center of mass — the balance point of the shape
Used for: distance calculations, representative points, labeling


luzern_centroid <- st_centroid(luzern)

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
For concave or C-shaped geometries, the centroid can fall outside the polygon
st_point_on_surface() always returns a point inside
Typical uses:

st_centroid(): Distance metrics, spatial analytics
st_point_on_surface(): Map labeling, feature sampling

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Three elementary operations

Affine transformations preserve lines and parallelism — angles and lengths may change
In sf: applied directly to sfc objects using arithmetic operators




Operation
sf syntax
Effect




Shift
sfc + c(dx, dy)
Move without changing shape


Scale
(sfc - p) * factor + p
Grow or shrink around a point p


Rotate
(sfc - p) * R(θ) + center
Rotate around a point p




The pattern (sfc - center) * operation + center appears in both scale and rotate: subtract center to bring the geometry to the origin, apply the transformation, then shift back. This is the key insight students should take away.

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Shift and Scale

# Shift: move 10 km east
luzern_shifted <- luzern_sfc + c(10000, 0)

# Scale: shrink to 75% around centroid
luzern_scaled  <- (luzern_sfc - luzern_center) * 0.75 + luzern_center

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Rotation

Shift to origin → rotate → shift back — otherwise the geometry rotates around (0, 0)
\(R(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\)


rotation <- function(deg) {
  r <- deg * pi / 180          # convert degrees to radians
  matrix(                      # 
    c(cos(r), -sin(r),          #   [ cos(r), -sin(r) ]
     sin(r), cos(r)),           #   [ sin(r),  cos(r) ]
    nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE
  )
}

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Why simplify?

Real datasets carry more vertices than any display scale needs
Excess vertices: slow rendering, large files, no visual benefit

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Challenge: Line simplification Algorithm


Given: a polyline V₁, V₂, …, Vₙ
Task: develop an algorithm that removes “unnecessary” vertices — those that add no meaningful shape information at scale ε








Closed book!


Do not use any external sources. Solve with your own ideas in groups

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Douglas-Peucker

st_simplify() uses the Douglas-Peucker algorithm
Core idea: a point is unnecessary if it lies close to the line between its neighbours
Tolerance ε controls how much deviation is acceptable






Step 1: draw baseline from first to last point







Step 2: find the farthest point — distance d = 3 > ε → keep it







Step 3: recurse on both halves independently







Step 4: continue recursion — more points kept or discarded







Step 5: result — only the essential vertices remain (blue)

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
The topology problem

st_simplify() processes each feature independently
Shared boundaries are simplified separately → gaps and overlaps appear

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Topology-preserving simplification

rmapshaper::ms_simplify() simplifies the whole layer at once — shared boundaries stay consistent
Uses the Visvalingam algorithm: iteratively removes the vertex that creates the smallest triangle area


library(rmapshaper)
# We specify the proportion of points to keep
n_ms <- ms_simplify(neighbors, keep = 0.5)

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Summary

st_centroid() returns the geometric centre of mass — useful for distance calculations and analytics, but it can fall outside the shape for concave or C-shaped geometries. Use st_point_on_surface() when you need a point guaranteed to lie inside.
Affine transformations (shift, scale, rotate) preserve shape and angles. All three follow the same pattern in sf: shift to the origin, apply the transformation, shift back. sf lets you do this with ordinary arithmetic directly on sfc objects. Transformations are not commutative — order matters.
st_simplify() reduces vertex count using the Douglas-Peucker algorithm: it recursively removes vertices that deviate less than tolerance ε from the local baseline. It operates feature by feature, so shared boundaries between adjacent polygons can develop gaps and overlaps.
ms_simplify() (rmapshaper) uses the Visvalingam algorithm and processes the entire layer at once, keeping shared edges consistent. Prefer it whenever topology matters.

title: Solutions: Algorithmic Challenges
section: A bounding box is four numbers
text:
A bounding box is four numbers

The axis-aligned bounding box of a set of points is the smallest rectangle (with sides parallel to the axes) that contains all of them
Numerically: just four values

\[\text{BB} = (x_{\min},\ y_{\min},\ x_{\max},\ y_{\max})\]

Key insight: you never need to store the full point list — only the current extremes

title: Solutions: Algorithmic Challenges
Solutions: Algorithmic Challenges
text:
R implementation

stream <- matrix(c(
  2489750, 1117500,
  2506250, 1172500,
  2552750, 1223500,
  2498000, 1198000,
  2470000, 1145000
), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)

bb <- c(xmin = stream[1,1], xmax = stream[1,1],
        ymin = stream[1,2], ymax = stream[1,2])

for (i in seq_len(nrow(stream))) {
  bb["xmin"] <- min(bb["xmin"], stream[i, 1])
  bb["xmax"] <- max(bb["xmax"], stream[i, 1])
  bb["ymin"] <- min(bb["ymin"], stream[i, 2])
  bb["ymax"] <- max(bb["ymax"], stream[i, 2])
}
bb

title: Solutions: Algorithmic Challenges
text:
The intuition
Draw a ray from the point horizontally to the right (→ infinity):

Count how many polygon edges the ray crosses
Odd number of crossings → point is inside
Even number of crossings → point is outside

title: Solutions: Algorithmic Challenges
text:
Ray casting: the algorithm
For each edge of the polygon (vertex \(i\) → vertex \(i+1\)):

Does the edge straddle the horizontal line \(y = p_y\)? \[( y_i > p_y ) \ne ( y_{i+1} > p_y )\]
If yes: is the ray–edge intersection to the right of \(p_x\)? \[x_{\text{hit}} = x_i + \frac{(p_y - y_i)(x_{i+1} - x_i)}{y_{i+1} - y_i} > p_x\]
If both conditions hold → flip an inside boolean (starts FALSE)

Result: inside after all edges = TRUE if the point is inside.

title: Solutions: Algorithmic Challenges
text:
R implementation

point_in_poly <- function(px, py, vx, vy) {
  n <- length(vx)
  inside <- FALSE
  j <- n
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    if (((vy[i] > py) != (vy[j] > py)) &&
        (px < (vx[j] - vx[i]) * (py - vy[i]) / (vy[j] - vy[i]) + vx[i])) {
      inside <- !inside
    }
    j <- i
  }
  inside
}

# polygon: a rough triangle
vx <- c(1, 4, 2.5); vy <- c(1, 1, 4)

point_in_poly(2.5, 2,   vx, vy)  # inside  → TRUE

[1] TRUE

point_in_poly(0,   0,   vx, vy)  # outside → FALSE

[1] FALSE

point_in_poly(3.5, 3.5, vx, vy)  # outside → FALSE

[1] FALSE

title: Solutions: Algorithmic Challenges
text:
Edge cases







Situation
How to handle




Ray passes exactly through a vertex
Use strict > on one side, >= on the other — ensures each vertex is counted at most once


Point lies exactly on an edge
Technically undefined; most implementations return TRUE


Polygon is not closed
Close it: ensure last vertex = first vertex


Concave / complex polygons
Algorithm works unchanged — this is its strength over simpler methods

title: Geocomputation with Vector Data
text:
Why a standard?

Vector data is used in PostGIS, QGIS, R, Python, ArcGIS, GDAL, …
Simple Features (ISO 19125-1:2004) is the OGC standard all major spatial tools implement
It defines: geometry types, encoding, and spatial relationships

title: Geocomputation with Vector Data
text:
What is a feature?

A simple feature is defined […] to have both spatial and non-spatial attributes. Spatial attributes are geometry valued, and simple features are based on 2D geometry with linear interpolation between vertices.

— ISO 19125

title: Geocomputation with Vector Data
text:
Geometry types

18 types defined in the standard; 7 cover the vast majority of real-world data:





Table 1: Source: Pebesma (2018)











Type
Description
Dimensions




POINT
zero-dimensional geometry containing a single point
0


LINESTRING
sequence of points connected by straight, non-self-intersecting line pieces
1


POLYGON
sequence of points forming a closed, non-self-intersecting ring (with optional holes)
2


MULTIPOINT
set of points
0


MULTILINESTRING
set of linestrings
1


MULTIPOLYGON
set of polygons
2


GEOMETRYCOLLECTION
set of geometries of any of the above types
NA

title: Geocomputation with Vector Data
text:
The Earth is not flat

The Earth is approximated as an ellipsoid: slightly flattened at the poles, bulging at the equator
A datum defines which ellipsoid to use and how to orient it:

WGS84 — global datum, used by GPS and internet maps
CH1903+ / LV95 — Swiss national datum, optimized for Switzerland

The same point has different coordinates in different datums

title: Geocomputation with Vector Data
text:
Projections

A projection transforms 3D ellipsoid coordinates onto a flat 2D plane
Every projection distorts at least one property — there is no undistorted flat map:

Equal-area — preserves area; distorts shape and angles
Conformal — preserves local shape / angles; distorts area
Equidistant — preserves distance from a point; distorts area and shape

National systems (e.g. LV95 / EPSG:2056) are conformal, minimizing distortion locally

title: Geocomputation with Vector Data
text:
Spatial relationships as questions

Binary predicates return TRUE/FALSE for a pair of geometries
The question determines the correct predicate:

Is this building inside the flood zone? → st_within(building, zone)
Does this road cross the zone? → st_crosses(road, zone)
Does any part of this forest touch Luzern? → st_intersects(forest, luzern)

The same pair can satisfy multiple predicates — wrong choice gives silently wrong results

title: Geocomputation with Vector Data
text:
Named predicates









Predicate

When TRUE
Typical use case




intersects

Any overlap exists (broadest)
Initial spatial filter


disjoint

No overlap whatsoever
Exclusion / NOT queries


touches

Boundaries meet; interiors do not
Adjacent parcels, shared borders





intersects is almost always TRUE for non-trivial pairs — rarely the right predicate for a precise question

title: Geocomputation with Vector Data
text:
Named predicates









Predicate

When TRUE
Typical use case




within

All of A is inside B
Point-in-polygon, containment


contains

All of B is inside A
Inverse of within


overlaps

Interiors intersect; neither contains the other
Partial overlap of same-type features


crosses

Interior of A intersects interior of B in lower dimension
Road through a zone

title: Geocomputation with Vector Data
text:
Choosing the right predicate

# intersects: any part of the forest touches Luzern (including tiny overlap at the border)
wald_intersects <- st_filter(tlm_wald, luzern, .predicate = st_intersects)

# within: the *entire* forest polygon lies inside Luzern
wald_within <- st_filter(tlm_wald, luzern, .predicate = st_within)

nrow(wald_intersects)  # more: includes forests that merely touch the border

[1] 3852

nrow(wald_within)      # fewer: only forests completely inside

[1] 3729

Take one geometry, return a (possibly different type of) geometry:









Operation
What it does
Output type

title: Geocomputation with Vector Data
text:
Binary set operations

Set algebra on geometries — same logic as SQL set operations
st_union() on a single layer: dissolve / aggregate — analogous to GROUP BY in SQL




Operation
Returns
Set notation




st_intersection(A, B)
Parts where A and B overlap
A ∩ B


st_union(A, B)
All of A and B, merged
A ∪ B


st_difference(A, B)
Parts of A outside B
A  B


st_sym_difference(A, B)
Parts of A or B, but not both
A △ B

title: Geocomputation with Vector Data
text:
Operations can change geometry type

Output type depends on the geometry relationship, not just the operation
Intersecting two polygons can yield a polygon, a line, or a point:

Overlapping → polygon;
sharing only an edge → line;
sharing only a corner → point

Code expecting a polygon fails silently if inputs only touch

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
Today

S² and R² — two models of space, one hidden default
When flat breaks — antimeridian rendering and predicate failures
A polygon has two sides — the core challenge of spherical geometry
Semi-open boundaries — why adjacent polygons share more than a border
Discussion — when does it matter in practice?

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
Two models of space


R² (flat)

Points are (x, y) on an infinite plane
Used by GEOS — the geometry engine behind QGIS, PostGIS, sf historically
Assumes straight lines, Euclidean distances
Appropriate for projected CRS


S² (sphere)

Points are (lon, lat) on a unit sphere
Used by s2 — Google’s C++ spherical geometry library, wrapped by the s2 R package
Lines follow great circles; distances are geodesic
Appropriate for geographic CRS
Powers Google Maps, Earth Engine, and BigQuery GIS

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
The switch

Since sf version 1.0 (2021), geographic coordinates automatically use s2 instead of GEOS.
Same function call; different geometry engine; potentially very different results
The switch affects: st_area(), st_length(), st_distance(), st_buffer(), all predicates


sf_use_s2()        # check current engine

[1] TRUE



sf_use_s2(FALSE)   # switch to GEOS (flat, R²)
sf_use_s2(TRUE)    # switch back to s2 (spherical, S²)


This is the key lever. When students see unexpected results with geographic data, checking sf_use_s2() is a good first step. Most of the time s2 gives the right answer; occasionally an operation isn’t yet implemented and you need to fall back to GEOS.

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
When flat breaks: the antimeridian
Same two endpoints — completely different rendering:

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
When flat breaks: predicates
The same polygon, the same point — different answer:

sf_use_s2(FALSE)
st_contains(pol, pole)   # R²: pole is outside

Sparse geometry binary predicate list of length 1, where the predicate
was `contains'
 1: (empty)



sf_use_s2(TRUE)
st_contains(pol, pole)   # S²: pole is inside

Sparse geometry binary predicate list of length 1, where the predicate
was `contains'
 1: 1

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
Two regions from one ring
In R²: a polygon ring encloses a bounded area. The outside extends to infinity — obviously “outside.”
In S²: a ring on a sphere divides it into exactly two finite regions. There is no infinity. Which side is “inside” depends entirely on ring direction.

# Same 4 corners — different winding order
sq_ccw <- st_sfc(st_polygon(list(matrix(          # CCW → small region
  c(-10,-10, 10,-10, 10,10, -10,10, -10,-10),
  ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE))), crs = 4326)

sq_cw  <- st_sfc(st_polygon(list(matrix(          # CW  → large region
  c(-10,-10, -10,10, 10,10, 10,-10, -10,-10),
  ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE))), crs = 4326)


units::set_units(st_area(sq_ccw), "km^2")   # small square

4969697 [km^2]

units::set_units(st_area(sq_cw),  "km^2")   # rest of Earth

4969697 [km^2]

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
Ring direction

In S²: interior is the region to the left when walking the boundary
CCW ring (counter-clockwise) → interior is the small side — same as R²
CW ring (clockwise) → interior is the large side — the “rest of the globe”




Ring
R² behaviour
S² behaviour




CCW exterior
Standard polygon
Small-side interior


CW exterior
Invalid / hole
Large-side interior




st_as_s2(x, oriented = FALSE) auto-corrects ring direction, assuming the intended interior is less than half the sphere

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
Stop and think

You are building a global land cover database. One of the classes is ocean.

How would you represent the ocean as a geometry in a GIS?

Discuss in pairs. Consider:

What are its boundaries?
Can you define it as a simple polygon in R²?
What about in S²?

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
The shared edge problem
Adjacent polygons share an edge. Under S² (or GEOS with model = "closed"):

A point on the shared edge intersects both polygons
For spatial joins or point-in-polygon counts: double-counting


# Default: closed model — adjacent counties intersect each other
st_intersects(nc[1:3, ], nc[1:3, ], sparse = FALSE)

      [,1] [,2]  [,3]
[1,]  TRUE TRUE FALSE
[2,]  TRUE TRUE  TRUE
[3,] FALSE TRUE  TRUE



# Semi-open: each county only intersects itself
st_intersects(nc[1:3, ], nc[1:3, ], sparse = FALSE, model = "semi-open")

      [,1]  [,2]  [,3]
[1,]  TRUE FALSE FALSE
[2,] FALSE  TRUE FALSE
[3,] FALSE FALSE  TRUE

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
How different are measurements?
For typical geographic analyses: negligible.



Measure
Relative difference (s2 vs flat)
Absolute example




Area
±0.007%
~7 km² per 100 000 km²


Length
±0.013%
~13 m per 100 km


Distance
up to ~0.5%
~1–2 km over 500 km



For continental or global scale: not negligible. The antimeridian is the clearest failure case.

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
When to use each engine

sf_use_s2(TRUE)   # default — always correct for geographic CRS
sf_use_s2(FALSE)  # fall back to GEOS when:
                  #  • working with projected CRS (s2 adds no benefit)
                  #  • an operation is not yet in s2 (e.g. st_voronoi())
                  #  • debugging: compare results between engines

Rule of thumb:

Geographic CRS (degrees) → leave s2 on
Projected CRS (metres) → irrelevant which engine; GEOS is used anyway
Operation fails or warns → check if the operation is implemented in s2; fall back if needed

title: Spherical Geometry in sf
text:
Discussion challenge

Your colleague downloads Swiss municipality boundaries in EPSG:4326 and runs:

municipalities |>
  st_join(cantons, join = st_intersects) |>
  group_by(canton_id) |>
  summarise(total_pop = sum(pop))

Some municipalities on cantonal borders appear in two cantons and their population is counted twice.

What is causing this?
How do you fix it?
Are there cases where model = "closed" is actually the right choice?








Discuss in groups


No external sources — reason from what you know about s2 boundary models

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Scenario 1: Centroids and Point Placement
Analyse land cover polygons in Canton Luzern to understand when centroids misbehave.

1.1: Load all wetland polygons (“Feuchtgebiet”) within Canton Luzern. Compute their centroids using st_centroid(). How many wetland polygons are there?
1.2: Use st_within() to check whether each centroid lies inside its source polygon. What proportion of centroids fall outside?
1.3: For the first five wetlands whose centroid is outside, compute st_point_on_surface() as well. Map these polygons with both point types (centroid in red, point-on-surface in blue). What do you notice about the polygon shapes?

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Scenario 2: Affine Transformations
Apply shift, scale, and rotation to the Canton Luzern boundary.

2.1: Load the canton geometry. Drop Z coordinates with st_zm() and compute its centroid.
2.2: Create three transformed versions of the geometry:

Shifted 20 km to the east
Scaled to 50% of its original size around the centroid
Rotated 45° around the centroid (you will need to write a rotation() function)

2.3: Map all four versions (original + three transformations) side by side.
2.4 (Challenge): Compose two operations — shift 10 km east, then rotate 20° around the new centroid. Compare this with rotating first and then shifting. Are the results the same?

title: Vector Geometry Operations
text:
Scenario 3: Simplification
Compare how st_simplify() and ms_simplify() behave, and discover the topology problem.

3.1: Load forest polygons (“Wald”) within Canton Luzern. Apply st_simplify() with tolerances of 100 m and 1 000 m. How many vertices does each version have compared to the original?
3.2: Load five neighbouring European countries (Switzerland, Germany, France, Austria, Italy) using rnaturalearth::ne_countries(), transform to EPSG:3857. Apply st_simplify() with a tolerance of 50 000 m. Do gaps appear between countries?
3.3: Apply rmapshaper::ms_simplify() with keep = 0.1 to the same dataset. How do the shared borders compare?
3.4: Map all three versions (original, st_simplify, ms_simplify) side by side.

title: Spatial Aggregation & Areal Interpolation
text:
Declaring attribute support: st_agr()

st_agr(src)                          # NA = undeclared

      zone population income_avg 
      <NA>       <NA>       <NA> 
Levels: constant aggregate identity



st_agr(src) <- c(population = "aggregate",   # block, summable  → extensive = TRUE
                 income_avg = "constant")     # spatially constant → extensive = FALSE
st_agr(src)

      <NA> population income_avg 
      <NA>  aggregate   constant 
Levels: constant aggregate identity



"aggregate" — block support, summable total: use extensive = TRUE
"constant" — spatially constant or rate: use extensive = FALSE

Setting this suppresses the warning and lets sf propagate attribute semantics correctly through operations like st_intersection().
